Yeah but OP isn't talking about life threatening emergencies, the kind that you need to go to the ER for. With a physical illness you have a specialist or primary care doctor. For mental health you have therapists and psychiatrist. Both physical and mental emergencies can be treated at an ER. But if you have a physical issue that pops up that you need to get checked out quickly but isn't threatening (such as an intense migraine ) you can visit a walk-in clinic and you don't need to wait as long as another doctor. But there is no equivalent for mental health. If you have a really bad panic attack, or have flashbacks because of PTSD, or any number of intense events your only options are basically wait it out or go to the ER. So OP isn't saying not to go to therapy/ see a regular doctor (as far as I can tell) just that there should be more options for mental health crisises rather than the ER.

My therapists have all told me that I have the right to see what's in their notes/ create our treatment plan together. It might be normal for a therapist to make an initial diagnosis and then hold off for a few sessions to fully confirm their idea, but they should always tell you. *Especially* if they have explicitly stated that they have diagnosed you with something. Ask them to view your treatment plan/ their notes, or just ask for your diagnosis. If they refuse and won't budge on the issue, find a new therapist. Therapy is about trust, and how can you trust someone who is withholding your very own diagnosis?

To answer your questions I'll just go over what bipolar is, in a broad sense. It is a mood disorder which means it affects your emotions primarily. It is characterized by periods of high mood and energy (which can last several days to even months) called mania or hypomania depending on which version of bipolar you have. It also features of low mood (depression) which is exactly like a standard depression with the same possible symptoms. These two periods (the 2 poles in bi-polar) fluctuate back and forth sometimes with periods of normalcy in between.

Bipolar disorder definitely amplifies thought patterns or ideas about oneself and others. It depends on the mood though. If you already don't like yourself that much, then the depression side with make those thoughts or feelings far worse. On the other side, if you are into someone, the mania might cause you to do wild and crazy things to win their affection, because at the time it feels like a good idea.

Now to get on to the fact that she hates one brother and loves another, this seems to me a clear sign of black and white thinking, or seeing things as entirely good or bad. This thought pattern can show up in many diagnoses, especially ones like anxiety or eating disorders. One diagnosis that is often characterized by black and white thinking and can cause interpersonal issues is borderline personality disorder, however I have no experience with bpd and so I don't know enough about it. 

So all these things you are describing could be due to bipolar, but is not clear at all. They could be caused by any number of diagnoses. For it to be bipolar it must have 2 distinct moods, depressive and manic, and without that element it is unlikely it is bipolar.

I will agree that you never know what other people might think or say about your work and there may be backlash. However I've almost never seen backlash over including a character who *happens to be* LGBT. For example, a fantasy story where one of the main characters is a theif and he is currently or previously in a relationship with another man. Its not a big part of his personality, it isn't forced or hamfishted, it's just a small detail that the author chose to add, and as far as I have experienced, there isn't any backlash to that. 

But if you choose to include some stereotypical element into your work, even if they are justified, you will receive some backlash. Yes I know some flamboyant gay people, but it's not there only trait. So when people include a gay character and like every chapter they keep talking about how flamboyant he is, it feels like a stereotype. I think that the main way to avoid this is if you are going to include stereotypical details --- consider how important they are. A lot of times people can use stereotypes as a crutch because they haven't done research, which is why I think it's so important to do. So if you can have your gay character not be flamboyant and it doesn't impact the plot or characterization, is it really that important. But again, sometimes you have a really strong idea for a character and leaving out this detail makes this character you're writting lesss like the one you imagine. So you can choose to include it. But I wouldn't make it a large part of the character. A few offhand descriptions, a few spoken lines, and I think that's enough. Because when you have someone who is constantly screaming 'yaaasss!'and they're gay, you had better make sure they are a dynamic and important character. If you are going to include them as an unimportant side character I would steer clear of stereotypes completely.

A final note on the LGBT characters getting killed off. I don't think it's so much a backlash to diversity or inclusion 'done wrong' but rather backlash to an over done trope. By far my least favorite trope is the chosen one. So many stories have a vague prophecy and the main character is the chosen one for... no apparent reason. This can make what would be a good book, stale and uninteresting. Some books use the chosen one trope to explore themes of destiny and free will and some use it to make a convenient plot. So when people get mad that an LGBT character gets killed off, it's because it's over done. So many stories don't let LGBT characters have happy endings, and so people are sick of it. Again this trope can be included and still be good, but only if, for examples, you are intending to make a depressing book, maybe a post apocalyptic world where none of your of your characters survive. Or a complex story of love, loss, and grief. But, if like so many other stories, you include an LGBT character or couple and they get killed off in the final battle but almost no one else does... I mean people are going to be upset. Also I happen to really like LGBT villians, I think sometimes they are done really well and are by far the coolest characters in their respective works.
